# Full projective coordinates: exact arithmetic, weights, and surviving inequalities

This note analyzes the full projective map suggested by a positive circuit
common term. It proves the transformed incidence and measure formulas and
a projectively invariant weighted Brunn-Minkowski inequality. Sections 4
and 5 assume `d>=1`; the measure transport and incidence formulas also
cover counting measure. It does not
claim that the transformed sharp depth inequality is independently known:
for the class specified below it is equivalent to OC itself.

## 1. An invertible chart requires a nonzero constant term

Let `ell(z)=a dot z+b` and work in the chart `ell(z)>0`. The formula

    F(z,x)=(u,y)=(z/ell(z),x/ell(z))                (1)

is invertible only if `b!=0`. If `b=0`, its integer-coordinate image
satisfies `a dot u=1`, and dimension is lost; for example with `n=d=1`
and `ell(z)=z`, points `(1,1)` and `(2,2)` both map to `(1,1)`.

If the chart contains a relevant integer fiber `z_0`, translate the
integer origin by `z_0` first. This preserves `Z^n x R^d` and replaces
the constant term by `ell(z_0)>0`. Thus the useful case can legitimately
be normalized to `b>0`. If there is no integer point in the chart, there
is no sampled measure there to study.

Define

    D(u)=1-a dot u.

Then the image chart is `D(u)>0`, and the inverse is

    z=b u/D(u), x=b y/D(u), ell(z)=b/D(u).          (2)

These identities follow directly from
`a dot u=(ell(z)-b)/ell(z)`. The projective map sends segments to
segments with a positive reparameterization on this chart, hence
preserves convexity. Its inverse has the same property. A compact convex
body wholly contained in the open chart has `ell` bounded away from zero,
so its image is again a compact convex body. If one first intersects a
body with the open chart and approaches `ell=0`, the image can instead
be unbounded; compactness must not be assumed in that situation.

## 2. Exact transformed lattice incidence

The mixed lattice in the chart becomes

    Omega x R^d,
    Omega={z/ell(z):z in Z^n,ell(z)>0}.             (3)

Equivalently, a chart point `u` is in `Omega` precisely when
`b u/D(u)` is integral. The set is discrete and relatively closed inside
`D>0`, because its inverse image under the continuous homeomorphism (2)
is the integer lattice in the original chart. It may accumulate at the
chart boundary, so it is not asserted to be a globally closed lattice.

For `z_0,z_1` in the chart put `L_j=ell(z_j)`, `u_j=z_j/L_j`. The image
of an original affine interpolation is

    F_z((1-lambda)z_0+lambda z_1)
      =[(1-lambda)L_0 u_0+lambda L_1 u_1]
         /[(1-lambda)L_0+lambda L_1].              (4)

In particular, when `z_0,z_1` have the same coordinatewise parity, the
integer midpoint is sent to

    u_m=(L_0 u_0+L_1 u_1)/(L_0+L_1),              (5)

which need not be the ordinary midpoint. The continuous coordinates obey
the identical weighted formula. In terms of `D_j=D(u_j)=b/L_j`, the
binary projective midpoint operation on full image points is

    (u_0,y_0) star (u_1,y_1)
      =[D_1(u_0,y_0)+D_0(u_1,y_1)]/(D_0+D_1).    (6)

This is exactly `F((F^{-1}(w_0)+F^{-1}(w_1))/2)`.

The loss of ordinary midpoint incidence is already visible for
`n=1,ell(z)=z+1`, whose chart integer indices are `z=0,1,2,...`.
Then `Omega={k/(k+1):k>=0}`. Same-parity indices zero and two map to
zero and `2/3`. Their ordinary midpoint `1/3` has inverse coordinate
`1/2`, so it is not in `Omega`. Their correct projective midpoint is
`1/2`, the image of the integer index one.

## 3. Exact fiber weights and closed-cap transport

On the fiber indexed by `z`, the continuous map is the homothety
`x->x/L_z`. Thus its geometric `d`-volume changes by `L_z^{-d}`.
The **pushforward measure**, however, must compensate with the opposite
power. If original mixed volume is `mu(A)=sum_z vol_d(A_z)`, then

    (F_*mu)(A')=sum_{u_z in Omega} w(u_z) vol_d(A'_{u_z}),
    w(u)=[b/D(u)]^d=L_z^d.                        (7)

For intrinsic `H_q` on a finite mixed union, the same identity holds with
`d` replaced by `q`; each positive `q`-dimensional fiber scales by
`L_z^{-q}`. For `q=0`, the compensating weight is one and counting
measure is preserved. Lower-dimensional fibers may have zero measure
but their supported points and their lattice incidence are still mapped.

An original closed halfspace

    alpha dot z+beta dot x>=c

becomes, after substitution of (2) and multiplication by positive `D`,

    (b alpha+c a) dot u+b beta dot y>=c.           (8)

Conversely every halfspace in the image chart has this form under the
inverse map, except that a halfspace bounded by the excluded chart
hyperplane can restrict to the whole chart or the empty set. Such trivial
restrictions do not change a depth infimum at a supported point. Therefore
the normalized depth of every individual supported point is exactly
preserved under (1), provided the image uses the weights (7). This
statement includes oblique halfspaces and closed boundaries: it is an
exact equality of measurable sets and pushforward measures, not a limit.

The weight in (7) is log-convex in `u`, not log-concave:

    log w=d log b-d log D,
    w^{-1/d}=D/b is affine.

Consequently ordinary theorems for sampled jointly log-concave densities
cannot simply be applied to this weighted image. The affine negative
power is an exact identity, not permission to ignore the transformed
discrete set or to identify a known sharp depth theorem for this class.

## 4. What happens to fiber-volume concavity

Let `C'=F(C)` and put

    f(u)=vol_d(C'_u)^{1/d},
    m(u)=w(u)vol_d(C'_u).

Ordinary Brunn-Minkowski makes `f` concave on the projection of `C'`.
Hence the exact transformed functional condition is

    [D(u)/b] m(u)^{1/d}=f(u) is concave.            (9)

For an ordinary interpolation `u_t=(1-t)u_0+t u_1`, write
`D_t=(1-t)D_0+tD_1`. Formula (9) says

    m(u_t)^{1/d}
      >=[(1-t)D_0 m(u_0)^{1/d}
          +tD_1 m(u_1)^{1/d}]/D_t.                (10)

At the projectively interpolated point (4), this becomes the original
ordinary concavity inequality

    m(u_lambda)^{1/d}
      >=(1-lambda)m(u_0)^{1/d}+lambda m(u_1)^{1/d}. (11)

Thus the power-concavity structure survives exactly when interpolation
weights are transformed together with the lattice. Neither `m^{1/d}`
nor `m` is thereby shown to satisfy the usual Euclidean sampled
concavity inequality at ordinary midpoints of `Omega`.

## 5. A projectively invariant weighted midpoint inequality

For two individual image fibers at indices corresponding to same-parity
`z_0,z_1`, let their continuous sets be compact positive-volume `A',B'`.
Their projective midpoint lies at the valid index (5), with continuous
set

    K'=(L_0 A'+L_1 B')/(L_0+L_1).

At that index, `L_m=(L_0+L_1)/2`. Brunn-Minkowski therefore gives

    [w(u_m)vol_d(K')]^{1/d}
      >=([w(u_0)vol_d(A')]^{1/d}
           +[w(u_1)vol_d(B')]^{1/d})/2.            (12)

Indeed the left side is
`(1/2)vol_d(L_0 A'+L_1 B')^{1/d}`, and the ordinary Brunn-Minkowski
lower bound is exactly the right side. This is a genuine invariant
inequality, with its arithmetic and every volume factor explicit.

It also extends to compact sets with finitely many fibers in a common
inverse parity class. Define `A' star B'` pointwise by (6), and let
`nu=F_*mu` be (7). Then

    nu(A' star B')^{1/d}
      >=(nu(A')^{1/d}+nu(B')^{1/d})/2.              (13)

For completeness, the finite-fiber proof can be given before transport.
Order the fibers of `A=F^{-1}(A')` and `B=F^{-1}(B')` by a generic
linear functional on their finite integer supports. Write their masses
as `a_i,b_j`, and their totals as `a,b`. Partition `[0,1]` consecutively
into pieces of lengths `a_i/a` and separately into pieces of lengths
`b_j/b`; let `q_ij` be the lengths of the overlapping pieces. Nonzero
overlaps form a monotone chain in `(i,j)`, so the associated integer
sums, and therefore their valid midpoint indices, are distinct.
Moreover `a_i>=q_ij a` and `b_j>=q_ij b`. Brunn-Minkowski gives mass at
the corresponding midpoint fiber at least

    2^{-d}(a_i^{1/d}+b_j^{1/d})^d
      >=2^{-d}q_ij(a^{1/d}+b^{1/d})^d.

Sum over the distinct midpoint fibers and use `sum q_ij=1`. Finally
transport by the exact pushforward identity (7) to obtain (13). This
proof does not invoke OC or a depth theorem.

An ordinary-midpoint version is false. In the one-dimensional example
after (6), let `A'={0}x[0,1]` and `B'={2/3}x[0,1]`, with `d=1`.
Their weighted masses are one and three. Their ordinary Minkowski
midpoint has integer-coordinate value `1/3`, outside `Omega`, and hence
zero sampled measure. Their projective midpoint instead has index `1/2`,
interval `[0,1]`, and weight two. It realizes equality in (12).

## 6. Helly number survives, but supplies its ordinary constant

The Helly number of `Omega x R^d` within the chart is exactly

    2^n(d+1).                                     (14)

For the upper bound, intersect any finite family of convex test sets
with the image chart, apply the inverse projective map, and use the
usual mixed-integer Helly theorem. Feasibility of every subfamily is
preserved exactly. Thus the transformed arithmetic has not acquired a
smaller Helly number.

For sharpness, choose a translated integer unit cube lying strictly in
the original chart and take its `2^n` vertices times the `d+1` vertices
of a continuous simplex. For each such product vertex `w`, take the
convex hull of all other product vertices. Any subfamily omitting the
set belonging to `w` has the common mixed point `w`. The full family has
no mixed point: its integer projection restricts to cube vertices, and
at each such fiber the `d+1` simplex facets opposite its vertices have
empty intersection. The sets lie within the chart; their projective
images prove the lower bound in (14). For `n=0`, the same construction
is the usual simplex Helly example. The mixed Helly theorem applied to
arbitrary finite measures yields its usual `1/[2^n(d+1)]` depth bound,
not the sharper `gamma_d/2^n` solely from (14).

## 7. The exact transformed sharp theorem is equivalent to OC

For compact convex bodies inside the chart in the full-volume case
`q=d`, the following two statements are equivalent by (7)-(8):

* the original mixed-integer depth bound `gamma_d/2^n`;
* the same bound for convex image bodies, constrained centers in
  `Omega x R^d`, and the weights `(b/D)^d`.

This is equality of depth at corresponding points, not merely a lossless
estimate. In the intrinsic case, use weights `(b/D)^q` instead and keep
the requested constant `gamma_d/2^n`; the same pointwise equivalence
holds. Conversely, arbitrary original compact bodies can be moved
into any fixed nonconstant positive chart by a sufficiently far integer
translation in a direction where `a dot z` increases. For a constant
positive `ell`, the transform is already an affine scaling of the
original problem. Therefore a universal sharp theorem for this exact
projective weighted class is not an independently weaker missing lemma.
It is a reformulation of OC and must not be cited as an established
generalized centerpoint theorem.

The standard sharp product example also transports exactly: translate
`[0,1]^n x T`, with a simplex `T`, by an integer vector until it is
contained in the chart. Its image has maximum weighted depth
`gamma_d/2^n`. Its image fibers generally have unequal Euclidean volumes;
the compensating weights are part of the equality example.

## 8. Why dividing only the continuous coordinate is insufficient

The map `(z,x)->(z,x/ell(z))` is not the full projective map and does
not preserve ambient halfspaces. With `ell(z)=z+1`, the halfspace
`x>=1` becomes `y>=1/(z+1)`, whose boundary is a curve. It need not
preserve convexity either: the rectangle `[0,2]x[0,1]` becomes

    {(z,y):0<=z<=2,0<=y<=1/(z+1)}.

The points `(0,1)` and `(2,1/3)` belong to this image, but their midpoint
`(1,2/3)` does not, since the allowed upper endpoint at one is `1/2`.
Thus a fiber-only division cannot be used to simplify circuit terms
while pretending that convexity and the ambient halfspace family remain
unchanged.

The rational identities and the midpoint/partial-map counterexamples are
checked in `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_full_projective_fiber_transform.py`.
